subject: dermatology
title: Skin structure, lesions and bedside tests

steps.tx: The epidermis has four layers over most of the body, and five on palms and soles. From deep to superficial they are the **stratum basale**, spinosum, granulosum and corneum, with stratum lucidum added on palms and soles. Keratinocytes are the principal cells and are present in all layers. Keratinocytes divide in the basal layer and mature as they move upward.

steps.tx: Other epidermal cells are important for exams. **Melanocytes** sit in the stratum basale, make melanin and pass it to keratinocytes, which protects against ultraviolet rays. **Merkel cells** in the basal layer mediate touch. **Langerhans cells** sit in the stratum spinosum, act as antigen presenting cells and contain tennis racquet shaped Birbeck granules.

steps.tx: Skin lesions are primary or secondary. Primary lesions include the **macule**, papule, plaque, nodule, vesicle, bulla, wheal and purpura. Secondary lesions are changes that develop later, such as scale, crust, erosion, ulcer, atrophy and **lichenification**. A flat discolouration up to 1 cm is a macule, and a raised solid lesion under 1 cm is a papule.
steps.say: Skin lesions are primary or secondary. Primary lesions include the macule, papule, plaque, nodule, vesicle, bulla, wheal and purpura. Secondary lesions are changes that develop later, such as scale, crust, erosion, ulcer, atrophy and lichenification. A flat discolouration up to one centimetre is a macule, and a raised solid lesion under one centimetre is a papule.

steps.tx: The **Koebner phenomenon** is isomorphic response, where morphologically identical lesions appear in traumatised normal skin. True isomorphic examples are psoriasis, lichen planus and vitiligo. Infections such as molluscum and warts show a pseudo-Koebner response. **Auspitz sign**, pinpoint bleeding after scale removal, is seen in psoriasis. **Darier sign** is urticarial wheal on stroking, seen in urticaria pigmentosa.

steps.tx: **Nikolsky sign** is positive when gentle rubbing causes epidermal separation, seen in pemphigus vulgaris. Blisters separate at different levels: subcorneal bullae rupture most easily, intraepidermal bullae have a thin roof, and dermoepidermal bullae have a thick roof and rupture least readily. The **Tzanck smear** from the base of a fresh vesicle shows acantholytic cells in pemphigus and multinucleated giant cells in herpes simplex, herpes zoster and varicella.

steps.tx: A **Wood lamp** emits ultraviolet light at about 360 nm and is used to examine pigment and fungal fluorescence. A **KOH mount** dissolves keratin so fungal hyphae can be seen on skin scrapings. **Dermoscopy** magnifies pigmented lesions to aid melanoma assessment. Blaschko lines are invisible developmental lines, and linear inflammatory eruptions follow them.
